notes: Lynch's Fianna Fáil governs alone with an absolute majority (75 of 144 seats since June 1969); the template coalition slot 2 holds the Just Society reform wing of Fine Gael (Costello, FitzGerald) as the liberal force. Fine Gael stays in slot 14 and Labour in 3 as in MD. The IRA split of December 1969 is reflected by the traditionalist Provisionals in slot 6 and Goulding's Marxist Official IRA in slot 7; Sinn Féin (Mac Giolla, still unified on 1 Jan 1970) in slot 5. Slot 4 switches from the Irish Workers' Party to the reunited Communist Party of Ireland in March 1970. Blaney's republican hawks inside Fianna Fáil fill slot 20. Islamic slots use the small student and doctor milieu around Dublin's medical schools. SF/WP sprites not reused because the 1970 Sinn Féin predates both logos.

0.name: Knights of Columbanus
0.text:
The Knights of Columbanus are a secretive Catholic fraternal order founded in Belfast in 1915 by Canon James O'Neill. Organised in councils across the country, they count senior civil servants, doctors, lawyers, businessmen and Garda officers among their brothers, and they work hand in glove with Archbishop John Charles McQuaid of Dublin, the most powerful churchman in the state.

The Knights see Ireland as a Catholic nation that must be defended against communism, secularism, Freemasonry and permissive foreign influences. They back strict censorship, Church control of schools and hospitals and the constitutional ban on divorce, and they regard the Western alliance as the bulwark of Christian civilisation. Their leverage lies in discreet patronage: appointments, promotions and contracts quietly steered towards trusted brothers.

1.name: Fianna Fáil
1.text:
Fianna Fáil was founded in 1926 by Éamon de Valera, now President of Ireland, and has governed without a break since 1957. Jack Lynch, a former Cork hurling star who became Taoiseach in 1966, won an outright majority of 75 seats in June 1969. His cabinet unites cautious pragmatists such as Patrick Hillery with ambitious younger ministers like Charles Haughey at Finance and the republican hawks Neil Blaney and Kevin Boland.

The party stands for economic expansion through free trade, foreign investment and planning, for membership of the European Economic Community, military neutrality and the peaceful reunification of Ireland. Its strength rests on a formidable nationwide machine, the loyalty of small farmers, shopkeepers and workers, and the support of a growing class of builders and businessmen.

2.name: The Just Society
2.english: Just Society Wing of Fine Gael
2.text:
The Just Society is the reforming wing of Fine Gael, named after 'Towards a Just Society', the policy document Declan Costello persuaded the party to adopt for the 1965 election. Its standard-bearers are Costello himself, the economist Garret FitzGerald, elected for Dublin South-East in 1969, and Tom O'Higgins, the party's presidential candidate in 1966. They chafe under Liam Cosgrave's cautious, conservative leadership.

The group wants economic and social planning, a modern welfare state, fairer taxation and a more pluralist republic able to reach out to Northern Protestants. It favours entry into the European Economic Community and a working partnership with Labour to end Fianna Fáil's long rule. Its support lies among young professionals, academics and Dublin's educated middle class, and its leverage among journalists and in party policy debates.

3.name: Páirtí an Lucht Oibre
3.text:
The Labour Party was founded in 1912 by James Connolly, James Larkin and the Irish Trades Union Congress. Led since 1960 by Brendan Corish, it fought the 1969 election on the slogan 'The Seventies Will Be Socialist', won 17 per cent of the vote and 18 seats, and brought in new recruits such as Conor Cruise O'Brien, Justin Keating, David Thornley and Noël Browne. It is the third force in the Dáil and still refuses to enter coalition.

Labour calls for public ownership of key industries and banks, state planning, better housing, health and education, and a more secular state. It is sceptical of entry into the Common Market and opposes partition. Its base lies in the trade unions, Dublin's working class and the agricultural labourers of Leinster and Munster.

4.name: Irish Workers' Party
4.text:
The Irish Workers' Party is the small communist party of the Republic, founded in 1948 as the Irish Workers' League and renamed in 1962. Its general secretary Michael O'Riordan, a veteran of the Connolly Column in the Spanish Civil War, is preparing a merger with the Communist Party of Northern Ireland to restore a single all-Ireland communist party.

The party follows Moscow's line and calls for national independence, Irish unity, public ownership and withdrawal from every Western entanglement. It opposes entry into the Common Market and seeks a broad anti-imperialist front with the trade unions and the left of the republican movement. Its membership is tiny, but it has able activists in Dublin's unions and a voice in its paper, the Irish Socialist.

4.name: Communist Party of Ireland
4.text:
The Communist Party of Ireland was re-established in March 1970 when the Irish Workers' Party and the Communist Party of Northern Ireland reunited, ending the division of Irish communists that dated from the Second World War. Michael O'Riordan, the Spanish Civil War veteran, is general secretary, and the party is strongest among trade unionists in Belfast and Dublin.

Loyal to the Soviet Union, it campaigns for civil rights in the North, an end to partition, public ownership and resistance to the Common Market and NATO. It seeks a broad front with the unions and the Marxist leadership of the republican movement. Small in numbers, it relies on union influence, Moscow's backing and its role as an organiser of the left.

5.name: Sinn Féin
5.text:
Sinn Féin is the political wing of the republican movement, founded by Arthur Griffith in 1905 and led since 1962 by Tomás Mac Giolla from Gardiner Place in Dublin. Under the influence of the IRA chief of staff Cathal Goulding and Marxist advisers such as Roy Johnston, it has turned sharply to the left. The movement is splitting: traditionalists have already broken with the IRA leadership, and the January Ard Fheis will vote on ending abstention from Leinster House.

Sinn Féin wants a 32-county democratic socialist republic, co-operatives, nationalisation of banks and land, and a national liberation front with communists and trade unionists. It opposes the Common Market and NATO. Its activists lead housing agitation in Dublin, fishing-rights protests in the west and the civil rights struggle in the North.

6.name: Provisional Irish Republican Army
6.text:
The Provisional Irish Republican Army was formed in December 1969 by traditionalists who walked out when the IRA convention voted to recognise the parliaments in Dublin, Belfast and London. Its Provisional Army Council, with Seán Mac Stíofáin as chief of staff alongside Ruairí Ó Brádaigh and Dáithí Ó Conaill, accuses Cathal Goulding's leadership of leaving the Catholics of Belfast defenceless during the riots of August 1969.

The Provisionals are Catholic, conservative and fiercely anti-communist, but above all anti-British: they reject the partition settlement, every parliament it created and any compromise short of a 32-county republic. Their strength lies in Belfast's Catholic districts, among old IRA veterans in the border counties and Munster, and in the arms and money now coming from sympathisers in Ireland and America.

7.name: Official Irish Republican Army
7.text:
The Official IRA is the part of the Irish Republican Army that stayed loyal to chief of staff Cathal Goulding after the split of December 1969. Since the failed border campaign of 1956-1962, Goulding, Seán Garland and the Marxist intellectual Roy Johnston have tried to turn the underground army into a revolutionary socialist movement, and its convention has now voted to abandon the old policy of abstention.

The Officials see partition as a tool of British and American imperialism and seek a socialist republic built in alliance with communists, trade unionists and northern civil rights campaigners. They keep their weapons and discipline in reserve and look to the socialist world for sympathy and support. Their leverage lies in their arms dumps and a tight, centralised command.

8.name: Jam'iyyat al-Atibba' al-Ja'fariyya
8.text:
The Ja'fari Medical Fellowship is a small circle of Shia doctors and medical students from Iraq, Bahrain and Kuwait who train at the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland and in Dublin's teaching hospitals. They pray together in rented rooms, mark the mourning of Muharram and follow Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim of Najaf, whose family is under growing pressure from Iraq's Ba'athist regime.

The fellowship stands for a moderate, educated Shiism: professional excellence, communal charity, respect for the senior marja and peaceful advancement for Shia communities at home. It distrusts both Ba'athist secularism and clerical radicalism, and stays strictly out of Irish politics. Its leverage is modest, resting on the prestige of the medical profession and the careers its members will build on returning to the Gulf and Iraq.

9.name: Hizb al-Da'wa al-Islamiyya
9.text:
The Islamic Dawa Party is a clandestine Iraqi Shia movement founded in Najaf in the late 1950s by young clerics and laymen around Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. Since 1969 the Ba'athist government has hunted its members, and a few Iraqi doctors who come to Dublin to sit the surgical fellowship of the Royal College of Surgeons quietly carry its pamphlets and contacts abroad.

Da'wa seeks an Islamic state built on the jurisprudence of the Shia clergy and rejects Ba'athism, communism and Western liberalism alike. It organises in secret cells, recruits students and professionals and prepares for a long struggle against Baghdad. In Ireland it has no public face; its only leverage lies in the conviction of a handful of exiles and their links to the seminaries of Najaf and Karbala.

10.name: Dublin Islamic Society
10.text:
The Dublin Islamic Society was founded in 1959 by Muslim students, many of them from South Africa, Malaysia and the Indian subcontinent, who had come to study medicine and engineering in the capital. It is the only organised Muslim body in the Republic, serving a few hundred students, doctors and traders who gather for Friday prayers in rented rooms and private homes.

The society represents a conservative, mainstream Sunni Islam centred on worship, religious instruction for children, halal food and a Muslim burial ground. It avoids politics, cultivates good relations with the Catholic authorities and the state, and hopes that wealthy Muslim governments will fund a proper mosque. Its leverage is respectability: the professional standing of its members and their links to the embassies and benefactors of the Muslim world.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani and is banned across the Arab world for trying to win over army officers. In Dublin a few Jordanian and Palestinian students at the medical schools pass around its pamphlets and debate its ideas with fellow Arab students embittered by the defeat of 1967.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Muslim regime, and calls for a single caliphate governing by Islamic law that would unite the Muslim world and liberate Palestine. It shuns violence, preferring patient propaganda and the conversion of elites. In Ireland it has no structure or public presence; its influence is confined to a few student flats and the contacts its members will carry home.

12.name: Federation of Student Islamic Societies in the UK and Eire
12.english: Federation of Student Islamic Societies in the UK and Eire
12.text:
The Federation of Student Islamic Societies in the UK and Eire was founded in the early 1960s to link Muslim student associations across Britain and Ireland, reaching the Muslim students of Dublin's colleges and medical schools. Its leaders are mostly Malaysian, Pakistani and Arab postgraduates, many inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood and by Abul A'la Mawdudi's Jamaat-e-Islami.

FOSIS promotes Islam as a complete way of life, organises study circles, conferences and summer camps, and prepares students to return home as leaders of an Islamic revival. It favours preaching and education over revolution, opposes secular nationalism and communism, and keeps its distance from the governments of Muslim states. In Ireland its leverage is small but real: it shapes the outlook of the next generation of Muslim doctors and engineers.

13.name: An Roinn Airgeadais
13.text:
The Department of Finance is the most powerful arm of the Irish civil service. Under T. K. Whitaker, its secretary from 1956 to 1969 and now Governor of the Central Bank, it produced the 1958 study Economic Development that launched the Programmes for Economic Expansion and ended decades of protectionism. Charles Murray has succeeded Whitaker as secretary, serving the minister Charles Haughey.

The mandarins believe that prosperity depends on planning, free trade, foreign investment and fiscal discipline rather than on party politics. They steer Ireland towards the European Economic Community, back the Industrial Development Authority's courting of foreign firms and distrust both populist spending and republican adventures in the North. Their leverage is the purse: every policy of every department must pass through Merrion Street.

14.name: Fine Gael
14.text:
Fine Gael was founded in 1933 from Cumann na nGaedheal, the party of the pro-Treaty side in the Civil War, the National Centre Party and the Blueshirts. Led since 1965 by Liam Cosgrave, son of the Free State's first head of government, it won 50 seats in June 1969 and is the main opposition, though it has not governed since the second inter-party government fell in 1957.

The party stands for law and order, sound finance, private enterprise, the interests of farmers and professionals, and entry into the European Economic Community. It is firmly Catholic and anti-communist but deeply committed to the institutions of the state. Its base lies among larger farmers, the professional middle class and the towns, and its best hope of power is a coalition with Labour.

15.name: Federated Union of Employers
15.text:
The Federated Union of Employers was founded in 1942 to represent private employers in wage bargaining and has become the main voice of Irish business in industrial relations. Its members range from breweries, biscuit makers, banks and building firms to the new foreign-owned factories attracted by tax concessions. The bitter maintenance craftsmen's strike of early 1969 has left it determined to bring order to pay bargaining.

The FUE favours centralised national wage agreements, restraint in public spending, protection of profits and the attraction of foreign capital. It supports entry into the European Economic Community and works closely with Fianna Fáil ministers while keeping its lines open to Fine Gael. Its leverage lies in investment decisions, jobs and the confidence of the banks.

16.name: Dublin Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Dublin Chamber of Commerce was founded in 1783 and is the oldest business organisation in the country. It speaks for the merchants, importers, retailers, accountants and solicitors of the capital, a milieu where old Protestant commercial families sit beside a new generation of Catholic entrepreneurs, and its presidency rotates each year among leading firms.

The Chamber champions free trade, low taxation, lean government and an end to the protective tariffs that sheltered Irish industry for three decades. It welcomed the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Area Agreement and wants rapid entry into the European Economic Community. It distrusts state monopolies, rising rates and trade union power. Its leverage lies in its access to ministers, its reports on economic policy and the weight of Dublin commerce.

17.name: An Taisce
17.english: An Taisce – National Trust for Ireland
17.text:
An Taisce, the National Trust for Ireland, was founded in 1948 by the naturalist Robert Lloyd Praeger and a circle of scholars and gentry to protect the country's landscapes, wildlife and buildings. Since the Planning Act of 1963 it must be consulted on development, and in December 1969 conservationists and architecture students occupied Georgian houses in Hume Street to stop their demolition, a protest that has captured the public imagination.

The Trust stands for careful planning, protection of the countryside and coastline, preservation of Georgian Dublin and resistance to speculative development. It is non-party but increasingly critical of the property developers who are reshaping the capital. Its members are architects, naturalists, academics and Anglo-Irish landowners, and its leverage lies in planning objections, expert reports and the press.

18.name: Irish Transport and General Workers' Union
18.english: Irish Transport and General Workers' Union
18.text:
The Irish Transport and General Workers' Union was founded in 1909 by James Larkin and later led by James Connolly, whose Citizen Army drilled at its headquarters, Liberty Hall, before the Easter Rising. It is the largest union in the country, organising dockers, factory workers, farm labourers and public employees, and since 1969 it has been led by general president Fintan Kennedy and general secretary Michael Mullen.

The union is affiliated to the Labour Party and stands for full employment, higher wages, public enterprise and a socialist Ireland in the tradition of Connolly. Its leaders are sceptical of the Common Market and wary of national wage agreements that would tie their hands. Its leverage lies in its mass membership, its funds and its ability to shut down ports and factories.
18.wiki: Irish Transport and General Workers' Union

19.name: Irish Communist Organisation
19.text:
The Irish Communist Organisation was founded in the mid-1960s by Irish emigrant radicals in London around Brendan Clifford, who broke with the pro-Soviet communists over Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin. It has since shifted its activity to Dublin and Belfast, publishing dense theoretical pamphlets on Irish history and economics, among them a study of the economics of partition.

The ICO is anti-revisionist: it upholds Stalin's legacy, scorns Moscow's revisionism and the reformism of the Irish Workers' Party, and is increasingly drawn to the heretical view that Ulster Protestants form a separate nation. It has only a few dozen members, but its polemics provoke sharp debate among students and on the republican left. Its leverage lies in ideas rather than numbers.

20.name: The Donegal Mafia
20.text:
The Donegal Mafia is the nickname of the formidable electoral machine that Neil Blaney, Minister for Agriculture and Fisheries, has built in Donegal and lent to Fianna Fáil in by-election after by-election. Since the burning of Catholic streets in Belfast in August 1969, Blaney and his ally Kevin Boland, Minister for Local Government, have become the voice of the party's republican hawks; in December 1969 Blaney declared that Fianna Fáil had never ruled out the use of force.

The hawks want Dublin to arm and protect northern nationalists and to press Britain hard for an end to partition. They are populist, Catholic, rural and suspicious of the cautious Lynch and the Dublin establishment. Their leverage lies in the party's grassroots, the border counties and the pull of the republican cause.

21.name: National Socialist Irish Workers' Party
21.text:
The National Socialist Irish Workers' Party was founded in 1968 in Irishtown, Dublin, by Terence Allan-Byrne, who styles himself 'Commander' Byrne. It has only a handful of members, close ties to British neo-Nazis and affiliation to the World Union of National Socialists, and it has never contested an election.

The party preaches racial nationalism, anti-Semitism and hatred of communism, and dreams of an Ireland purged of Jews, immigrants and liberal influences. It sends threatening letters to members of the small Jewish community and to black residents and students, and trades in Nazi literature and memorabilia that Irish law does not restrict. It has no leverage beyond notoriety and the hope of exploiting sectarian violence in the North.

22.name: Óglaigh na hÉireann
22.text:
The Defence Forces are the army, naval service and air corps of the Irish state, commanded since 1962 by Lieutenant General Seán Mac Eoin, former commander of the UN force in the Congo. Their pride rests on peacekeeping in the Congo and Cyprus, but in August 1969 they were sent to the border to set up field hospitals and camps, and army intelligence officers have since been in contact with Catholic defence committees in the North.

The officer corps is loyal to the constitution and proud of its descent from the Volunteers of 1916. Yet it is underfunded and divided over the northern crisis. Its leverage lies in its monopoly of legitimate force and the fear that the troubles across the border could draw it in.

23.name: Ó Conchubhair Donn
23.text:
The O'Conor Don is the head of the O'Conors of Connacht, direct descendants of Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, the last High King of Ireland, who submitted to Henry II in 1175. The family seat is Clonalis House near Castlerea in County Roscommon, and the present holder of the title, Father Charles O'Conor, is a Jesuit priest. Like other Gaelic chiefs, he enjoys courtesy recognition from the Chief Herald of Ireland.

In a republic born of revolution, monarchism is a curiosity rather than a cause. A few revivalists and romantics nevertheless dream of a restored High Kingship as a native, Catholic alternative to both the British crown and party politics. The dynasty's leverage is purely symbolic: an ancient name, a historic house and the sentiment of the west.
